I therefore remain largely unsupported and there remains much controversy whether reduced surface area of appendages provides energetic savings sufficient to make this morphological trend truly adaptive.

ROUND 3: POTD 2 prelim  

Kofi and Dela take 2 hours to complete a job. Dela and Fuseini take 3 hours to do the job. Fuseini and Kofi take 4 hours to do the job. How long will it take all three working together to complete the job?

SOLUTION:
              Time     Rate  
Kofi          a         1/a         
Dela         b         1/b                                        
Fuseini     c         1/c

   1/a + 1/b = 1/2,       (1 MARK)

   1/b + 1/c = 1/3,       (1 MARK)

   1/c + 1/a = ¼            (1 MARK)

   1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 1/T (T is time taken by all three)   (2 MARKS)

   2(1/a + 1/b + 1/c) = ½ + 1/3 + ¼ = (6 + 4 + 3)/12 = 13/12  (2 MARKS)

  2(1/T) = 13/12, 1/T = 13/24    

  T = 24/13                                     (2 MARKS)

   Hence all three will take 24/13 hours   (1 MARK)

A(1, 2), B(-1, 4) and C(2, 4).

SOLUTION:

A(1, 2):   a + b + c = 2           (i)

B(-1, 4):  a – b + c = 4           (ii)

(i) – (ii)  2b = - 2, b = -1                       (1 MARK)

Equation is y = x2 – x + 2                    (1 MARK)

Intercept on the y-axis, x = 0, y = 2, hence (0, 2)   (1 MARK)

ROUND 3: POTD 4 national

Solve for x a real number, from the equation 4x + 16x = 64x (Hint: Let u = 4x)

SOLUTION:

Let u = 4x, u2 = 16x, u3 = 64x                                             

u + u2 = u3,                                                          (2 MARKS)

u3 – u2 – u = u(u2 - u – 1) = 0      

u = 0, or u2 – u – 1 = 0                                      (2 MARKS)

u = 0, 4x = 0 has no solution                            (1 MARK)

Describe the following types of mutations and identify the potential effects of each type.
Chromosomal alterations 
They are mutations that cause major changes in the structure of chromosomes. They are very serious and often result in the death of the organism in which they occur. If the organism survives, it may be affected in multiple ways. 

Point mutations 
They are changes in a single nucleotide. Their effects depend on how they change the genetic code and may range from no effects to serious effects. 

Frameshift mutations 
They change the reading frame of the genetic code. They are likely to have drastic effects on the encoded protein.

RR and Rr would express the dominant R phenotype because only one dominant allele (in this case, R) is needed to express the dominant phenotype.

R and r cannot be on different loci because they are alleles of the same gene.

No, because there is only one version of a gene on a single chromosome. They are on homologous chromosomes.

Why should the presence of a protein (such as albumin) in the urine of an individual be a cause for concern? 
Proteins such as albumin are not usually filtered out of the blood in the glomeruli of the kidneys. When the glomerular capillaries are damaged, it allows albumin to leak into the filtrate from the blood. As a result, albumin ends up being excreted in the urine. Therefore, the presence of proteins such as albumin in the urine is a cause for concern because it may indicate that there is a problem with kidney function.

What is genetic engineering?
It is the artificial manipulation, modification, and recombination of DNA or other nucleic acid molecules in order to modify an organism or population of organisms.

A human gene inserted into bacteria still produces the same human protein because the genetic code is universal, meaning that it is the same among all living organisms.

What is gene therapy and why is it considered a type of biotechnology?
It is the introduction of a normal gene into an individual’s genome in order to repair a mutation that causes a genetic disease. / In gene therapy, a normal gene is inserted into human cells to compensate for an abnormally functioning gene. 
Gene therapy is a type of genetic engineering because it involves changing the genetic makeup of an organism.

Problem of the Day 3
To determine the amount of ascorbic acid (vitamin C) in 500 cm3 of fruit juice purchased, a student reacts the ascorbic acid contained in the juice with an excess of iodine and back-titrates the excess iodine with thiosulphate solution. The student reacts 25 cm3 of orange juice with 30 cm3 of 0.080 moldm–3 of iodine. At the end of the reaction, the excess iodine required 20 cm3 of 0.20 moldm–3 of Na2S2O3. Determine the mass of ascorbic acid present in the fruit juice purchased. [C = 12 g/mol; O = 16 g/mol; H = 1.0 g/mol].
The equation of reactions are as follows:
C6H8O6 + I2  →  C6H6O6  + 2H–  + 2 I– 
I2 + 2 S2O32–  →   2I–   +  S4O62– 


SOLUTION
Number of moles of S2O32– = 0.020 × 0.2 = 0.0040 mol
From equation of reaction, number of moles of I2 = 0.0040/2 = 0.0020 mol
Moles of I2 added = 0.080 × 0.030 = 0.0024 mol
Hence moles of I2 which reacted = moles of C6H8O6 = 0.0024 – 0.0020 = 0.00040 mol
Moles of C6H8O6 in 500 cm3 of juice = 500 × 0.00040/25 = 0.0080 mol
Mass of ascorbic acid, C6H8O6 = 0.0080 × 176 = 1.408 = 1.41 g

Problem of the Day 4
The decay constant of a radioactive isotope is 1.155 × 10 –3 s–1. 
How long will it take 19.2 mg of the isotope to decay to 0.15 mg
Given an initial 25.6 mg sample of the radionuclide, what amount of radionuclide will decay after 3600 seconds. 
[Take ln 2 as 0.693]


SOLUTION
Half-life = 0.693/1.155 × 10–3 = 600 s = 10 minutes
19.2 mg to 0.15 mg occurs in 7 half-lives. 
Hence time taken = 7 × 10 minutes = 70 minutes = 4200 seconds

3600 seconds = 60 minutes = 6 half-lives 
After 6 half-lives amount of original 25.6 mg remaining will be 0.40 mg.
Amount decayed after 3600s = 25.6 – 0.40 = 25.2 mg

Problem of the Day 5
A 0.864 g sample containing silver was dissolved in 400 cm3 of water and reacted with 30.0 cm3 of 0.500 moldm–3 of potassium iodide solution. The resulting precipitate was carefully washed, dried to a constant mass, and weighed to obtain a mass of 0.470 g. Determine the percentage composition by mass of silver in the sample.
Given that, 200 mg of silver is required to make a coin, how many coins can be made from the sample given?
[K = 39.0 g/mol; I = 127 g/mol; Ag = 108 g/mol]

SOLUTION
Precipitate = AgI
Equation of reaction = Ag+ + I– → AgI (s)
Mass of AgI = 0.470 g
Molar mass of AgI = 235 g/mol
Moles of AgI = 0.470/235 = 0.00200 mol
Mass of Ag = 0.00200 × 108 = 0.216 g
Percentage of silver in sample = 0.216/0.860 × 100 = 25.0%

Sample contains 216 mg of silver. Hence only one coin can be made from sample.

What is meant by emasculation in plant breeding? Explain when and why a plant breeder employ this technique?

Answer
Emasculation is the process of removing anthers from bisexual flowers without affecting the female reproductive part (pistil), which is used in various plant hybridization techniques.

Emasculation is performed by plant breeders in bisexual flowers
It prevents self-pollination. 
This allows the breeder to obtain the desired variety of a plant by crossing a particular plant with the desired pollen grain. 
To remove the anthers, the flowers are covered with a bag before they open. 
This ensures that the flower is pollinated by pollen grains obtained from desirable plant varieties only (avoid self-pollination). 
Later, the mature, viable, and stored pollen grains are dusted on the bagged stigma by breeders to allow artificial pollination to take place and obtain the desired plant variety.

Contest 40c
State the effect(s) of each of the following on biodiversity (the variability among living organisms from all source.

 Habitat loss
Habitat loss will decrease biodiversity. When this occurs only the animals that are able to adapt and live within the new habitat will survive. This could potentially cause a genetic bottleneck for those that were once thriving in the initial habitat.

Overharvesting
Overharvesting can limit biodiversity. If too much of a species (whether plants or animals) is harvested for human use, then there is the potential that certain genes from the pool are completely wiped out. This means that they will be very hard to re-introduce into the population, and the biodiversity lessens.

Exotic species
Exotic species are a threat to biodiversity. This is because it will add a new element to the food chain. Perhaps the exotic species is a predator and will kill off some other organisms therefore shrinking biodiversity in an area. The exotic species could also be an invasive plant that takes root space away from other species, therefore threatening biodiversity.

Ans:	The atomic radius decreases smoothly from left to right up to the halogen.

Ans:	Three of the boron orbitals undergo sp2 hybridisation, each hybridised orbital singly occupied. The three orbitals are uniformly spread around boron giving a trigonal plane with the boron at the centre . The remaining empty p-orbital is perpendicular to the plane.

Ans:	The orbitals of oxygen atom undergo sp3 hybridisation, two of the orbitals containing electron pair each, the other two singly occupied. Ans:	Though the first ionisation energy of an element depends on atomic radius, other factors such as effective nuclear charge is also important. Ans:	Sodium and potassium are in the same Group of the Periodic Table. Down the Group, atomic radius increases. The attractive force on the valence electron decreases from sodium to potassium. Hence, potassium has the lower first ionisation energy.

Boyle’s Law states that the volume of a gas varies inversely with its pressure at constant temperature. How does the Kinetic Theory of gases explain this law? 
Ans:	At constant temperature, the average kinetic energy of a molecule is constant. Therefore, the average speed of the molecule is constant and the force of collision with walls, generating the pressure is constant. When the volume is increased the concentration decreases and the frequency of collision per unit wall area decreases leading to decrease in pressure. 
Avogadro’s Law states that equal volumes of any two gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. How does the Kinetic Theory of gases explain this law?
Ans:	Since the pressure of a gas at a given temperature results from the frequency of collisions with the walls of its container, for two different gases of the same volume and at the same temperature to have the same pressure, the frequency of collisions should be the same and hence should contain the same number of molecules.  
Charles’ Law states that the volume occupied by any given amount of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. 
Ans:	When temperature is raised, the average molecular speed of the molecule is increased, frequency of collision with the walls of its container is increased and the pressure is increased, all other factors remaining constant. If the pressure is to remain constant the volume has to increase to reduce the frequency per unit wall area.

Explain how two liquids of different boiling points get separated in a simple distillation procedure. 
Ans:	When the mixture is heated the liquid with the lower boiling point begins to vapourise. This continues until the boiling point is reached. The vapour is 100% of that of the liquid with a lower boiling point. The vapour enters the condenser and gets collected as liquid. The second liquid distils at a higher temperature.
Explain how two liquids with close boiling points get separated by fractional distillation. 
Ans:	When the mixture is initially heated the vapour of the liquid of the lower boiling point constitutes a bigger fraction of the vapour that rises. As the vapour rises in the fractionating column it becomes richer and richer of the vapour of the low boiling liquid. The vapour finally becomes pure vapour of the lower boiling liquid; it enters the condenser and condenses as pure liquid. The second liquid distils later.   
Explain how the fractionating column gets the vapours separated. 
Ans:	The fractionating column offers a larger surface for condensation and re-evaporation processes. When the mixture of vapours enters the column, it condenses and as the liquid descends it meets hot vapour and re-evaporation takes place. The new vapour, richer in the vapour of the lower boiling liquid, rises and re-condenses. The process repeats itself further up the column until pure vapour of the lower boiling liquid enters the condenser. Generally, the temperature in the column decreases as the vapour ascends the column

The first ionisation energy of elements generally increases from left to right in a Period of the Periodic Table, that is in the order of increasing atomic number.  In that case why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen. Oxygen has a higher atomic number. 
Ans:	Oxygen has a p4 subshell electron configuration in the neutral atom and loses an electron readily to form a more stable half-filled p3 subshell. The neutral atom of nitrogen on the other hand has a p3 subshell which is stable and losing an electron is energetically not that favourable. 
Hydrogen has a lower first ionisation energy than helium although hydrogen has a smaller atomic radius. How can this be justified? 
Ans:	Though the first ionisation energy of an element depends on atomic radius, other factors such as effective nuclear charge is also important. The net attractive force of the two protons on the valence electrons in helium is much greater than the attractive force of one proton on one valence electron in hydrogen. Hence the first ionisation energy of helium is bigger.    
Explain why sodium has a higher first ionisation energy than potassium? 
Ans:	Sodium and potassium are in the same Group of the Periodic Table. Down the Group, atomic radius increases. The attractive force on the valence electron decreases from sodium to potassium. Hence, potassium has the lower first ionisation energy.

Atomic size of elements is a Periodic Property. Use a Period of the Periodic Table to illustrate this. 
Ans:	In a Period, atomic size decreases from left to right. In a Period, from an element to the next, the electron enters the same valence shell while the nuclear charge increases by one. The valence electrons are therefore attracted with a greater force ( or effective nuclear charge increases) leading to a decrease in atomic radius.  
Use a Group of the Periodic Table to illustrate the fact that the first ionization energy is a Periodic Property. 
Ans:	As one descends a Group in the Periodic Table, the first ionization decreases. From one element to the one below it, a shell (or an energy level) is added. This is farther away from the nucleus. The electrons in the outer shell therefore experience less attractive force of the nucleus.   
Enthalpy of Atomization energy is another Periodic Property of elements. Use Group (III) or 13 of the Periodic Table to illustrate this. 
Ans:	The atomization energy of the elements in Group (III) or 13 decreases down the Group. It reflects the strength of interatomic bonds. In boron, we have strong covalent bonds whereas, from aluminium down to thallium, it is metallic bonds. Down the Group, the atoms get bigger and the binding energies decrease.

Explain why the compound CH3COOH is an acid but CH3CH2OH is not. 
Ans:	Acidity depends on	(i) ability to donate H+ ions and 	(ii) the stability of the anion formed.
The OH bonds in each of the compounds is polarized.  But when CH3CH2OH loses a proton the conjugate base CH3CH2O- is not stable and so readily recombines with H+ to form CH3CH2OH. When CH3COOH loses a proton, the conjugate base is stabilized by resonance.

Ans:	As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of the particles in the gas
		increases. They strike the surface with greater force giving rise to increase 
		in pressure. Since the external pressure is constant, the volume increases 
		until internal and external pressures are balanced.	
Boyle’s law which states that at a constant temperature, the pressure of a given mass of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume. 
Ans:	When the volume of a given quantity of a gas is reduced, there is a 
		corresponding decrease in surface area so there is an increase in frequency 
		of collision of the particles with the surface although the speed of the 
		particles remain the same. More frequent collisions lead to increase in 
		pressure.
Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressures which states that at constant volume and temperature the total pressure of a mixture of gases is the sum of individual pressures (or partial pressures) 
Ans:	Since particle sizes of gases are negligible compared to the volume, having 
		different particles in a given volume will not affect the movement and the 
		frequency with which each particle collides with the surface of the 
		container. Hence the total pressure will be the sum of the pressure each gas 
		would exert in the absence of others.

Ans:	Screening effect is the reduced attraction by the nucleus for the outermost electron caused by the core electrons.

Ans:	Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge that the outermost electrons feel through attraction by the nucleus.

There are five postulates of the Kinetic Molecular Theory. State any one of them and show how the postulate is manifested in the behaviour of gases. 
Ans:	Any one of the following 
Gases are composed of molecules/atoms whose size is negligible compared to the average distance between them. 
Implication:	Gases can easily be compressed
Molecules/atoms move randomly in straight lines in all directions and at various speed. 
Implication:	Brownian motion or pressure of a gas in container uniform on all the surfaces. 
The forces of attraction or repulsion between two molecules/atoms in a gas are very weak or negligible. 
Implication:	Gases fill any available space because of very small intermolecular forces. Also gases in a mixture behave independently. 
When molecules/atoms collide with one another the collisions are elastic. 
Implication:	Isolated quantity of a gas does not lose pressure. 
The average kinetic energy of a gaseous molecule/atom is proportional to temperature. 
Implication:	Brownian motion, pressure or volume increases with temperature.

Boyle’s Law states that the volume of a gas varies inversely with its pressure at constant temperature. How does the Kinetic Theory of gases explain this law? 
Ans:	At constant temperature, the average kinetic energy of a molecule is constant. Therefore, the average speed of the molecule is constant and the force of collision with walls, generating the pressure is constant. When the volume is increased the concentration decreases and the frequency of collision per unit wall area decreases leading to decrease in pressure. 
Avogadro’s Law states that equal volumes of any two gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. How does the Kinetic Theory of gases explain this law?
Ans:	Since the pressure of a gas at a given temperature results from the frequency of collisions with the walls of its container, for two different gases of the same volume and at the same temperature to have the same pressure, the frequency of collisions should be the same and hence should contain the same number of molecules.  
Charles’ Law states that the volume occupied by any given amount of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. 
Ans:	When temperature is raised, the average molecular speed of the molecule is increased, frequency of collision with the walls of its container is increased and the pressure is increased, all other factors remaining constant. If the pressure is to remain constant the volume has to increase to reduce the frequency per unit wall area.

Explain how two liquids of different boiling points get separated in a simple distillation procedure. 
Ans:	When the mixture is heated the liquid with the lower boiling point begins to vapourise. This continues until the boiling point is reached. The vapour is 100% of that of the liquid with a lower boiling point. The vapour enters the condenser and gets collected as liquid. The second liquid distils at a higher temperature.
Explain how two liquids with close boiling points get separated by fractional distillation. 
Ans:	When the mixture is initially heated the vapour of the liquid of the lower boiling point constitutes a bigger fraction of the vapour that rises. As the vapour rises in the fractionating column it becomes richer and richer of the vapour of the low boiling liquid. The vapour finally becomes pure vapour of the lower boiling liquid; it enters the condenser and condenses as pure liquid. The second liquid distils later.   
Explain how the fractionating column gets the vapours separated. 
Ans:	The fractionating column offers a larger surface for condensation and re-evaporation processes. When the mixture of vapours enters the column, it condenses and as the liquid descends it meets hot vapour and re-evaporation takes place. The new vapour, richer in the vapour of the lower boiling liquid, rises and re-condenses. The process repeats itself further up the column until pure vapour of the lower boiling liquid enters the condenser. Generally, the temperature in the column decreases as the vapour ascends the column

Ans:	Since particle sizes of gases are negligible compared to the volume, having 
		different particles in a given volume will not affect the movement and the 
		frequency with which each particle collides with the surface of the 
		container. Hence the total pressure will be the sum of the pressure each gas 
		would exert in the absence of others.

Define the term ‘Screening Effect’ used in connection with atoms and explain how Screening Effect is expected to vary across a Period of the Periodic Table.
Ans:	Screening effect is the reduced attraction by the nucleus for the outermost electron caused by the core electrons.
Across a Period, the outer electrons enter the same shell, and are shielded by the same core electrons. The screening effect will be constant across the Period.
Define the term ‘Effective Nuclear Charge’ and state how Effective Nuclear Charge will vary down a Group in the Periodic Table. 
Ans:	Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge that the outermost electrons feel through attraction by the nucleus. 
	As one moves down a Group, more core shells of electrons are added hence the effective nuclear charge decreases down the Group (i.e. more core electrons but the same number of outer electron).
Use Screening Effect and Effective Nuclear Charge to explain the variation of atomic radius across a Period in the Periodic Table 
Ans:	Across the same Period, the screening effect of the core electrons is constant but effective nuclear charge increases because the atomic number/ number of protons increases. Hence there will be an increasing attraction on the outer shell. Atomic radius decreases across the Period.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY 2018 FINALS   (POTD 13)

A salesperson for a furniture company can be paid in one of two ways for the furniture he/she sells.
PLAN A: a monthly salary of GHc900 plus a commission of 10% of sales
PLAN B: a monthly salary of GH1200 plus a commission of 15% of sales in excess of GHc8,000.
Assume that monthly sales always exceeds GHc8,000.  For what amount of monthly sales is

i) income from Plan A equal to that of Plan B? Find this monthly income.

ii) income from Plan B is better than that of Plan A?  


SOLUTION:
Let monthly sales be GHc x  where x > 8,000
Income from PlanA = 900 + 0.1x                                                 (1MARK)
Income from PlanB = 1200 + (0.15)(x - 8,000 )                         (1 MARK)

i) For equal incomes, we have
           900 + (0.1)x = 1200 + (0.15)(x - 8000 )                            (1 MARK)
                                 = 1200 – 1200 + (0.15)x
                                 = (0.15)x
                         900 = (0.05)x 
                            5x = 90000 and x = 18000                               (1 MARK)
The required monthly sales is GHc18,000                               (1 MARK)
The monthly income is 900 + (0.1)18000 = 900 + 1800 = GHc2700   (1 MARK)


ii) For Plan B to be better than plan A, we require

       1200 + (0.15)(x – 8000) > 900 + (0.1)x                                                    (2 MARKS)
                                    (0.15)x > 900 + 0.1)x
                                    (0.05)x > 900
                                            5x > 90000
                                              x > 18000                                                             (1 MARK)
Plan B is better than Plan A if monthly sales exceeds GHc18,000          (1 MARK)

QUESTION 12
Describe the mechanism of hearing in mammals.
Answer
The sound waves are directed towards the ear canal by the pinna.
The waves that enter the canal are concentrated and made to strike against the tympanum.
The vibrations are picked up by the malleus on the other side.
These vibrations are transmitted to the fenestra ovalis via the incus and the stapes.
The vibrations that strike the oval window are amplified
These vibrations travel along the vestibular canal to the end of the cochlea and then to the tympanic canal. The vibrations are also transmitted via the Reisnner's membrane to the basilar membrane and then to the tympanic canal.
Note that the vibrations travel along the vestibular and tympanic canals in the opposite directions.
From the basilar membrane the vibrations are picked up by the sensory hair cells of the organ of corti and transmitted as action potentials to the neurons of the auditory nerve fibres.
The action potentials are then transmitted as nerve impulses to the auditory cortex of the brain through the auditory nerve.
The brain then interprets it as sound

To determine the sensitivity of the body to temperature, an SHS student performed the experiment below
He collected three jars or beakers of about the same size and filled one with cold water (10-15 °C), one with hot water (40-50 °C) and the third with warm water (about 25 °C).  The first finger of the left hand was placed in the cold water and the first finger of the right hand in the hot water.  He left both fingers immersed for at least one minute. After one minute, he removed both fingers from the jars and dipped them repeatedly but alternately in the warm water for about a second at a time.
What impression did (i) the left finger, (ii) the right finger give about the temperature of the warm water? 
 Why should there be any difference in the sensory information from the two fingers?
How could you modify the experiment to test your suggestion in ‘2’ above? 
Does the result mean that the skin of the fingers is not capable of judging whether an object is hot or cold? 
What does the result suggest about the way in which the skin responds to temperature
Answer
The finger which has been immersed in cold water will register warmth. 
ii. The finger previously held in hot water will register coldness. 
The difference in sensations can be attributed to the difference in the temperature of the fingers after one minute's immersion. /
An alternative explanation is that the warmth receptors in the hot water become adapted, i.e. after prolonged immersion they no longer send impulses to the brain. Consequently, on transfer to lukewarm water, there are few impulses sent to the brain from the warmth receptors of this finger, whereas the warmth receptors in the cold finger fire normally.
This can be tested by repeating the experiment with the left-hand finger in the hot water and the right-hand finger in the cold water. The sensation on dipping them both into warm water should be the reverse of the first experiment.  
The results suggest that the fingers detect whether they are gaining or losing heat rather than the actual temperature of an object. Metal objects at room temperature will feel cold to the touch because heat is conducted away from the fingers, while wooden objects at the same temperature feel less cold. 
The results seem to imply that the thermo-receptors respond to change in temperature rather than to any particular temperature. In fact, there is a steady discharge of nerve impulses from cold and warmth receptors at all temperatures within certain limits but increased bursts of impulses occur during sudden changes of temperature.

Carbon – oxygen double bond is stronger than carbon – carbon double bond, why?

Define ‘Standard Enthalpy of Formation’ of a substance. 
Ans:	It is the enthalpy change for the formation of one mole of the substance in its standard state from the stable forms of its elements in their standard states under standard conditions of pressure and temperature(or at 298K and 100kPa).
Define ‘Standard Enthalpy of Combustion’ of a compound. 
Ans:	It is the enthalpy change when one mole of the substance is completely burnt in excess oxygen under standard conditions of pressure and temperature (or at 298K and 100kPa). 
Define ‘Standard Enthalpy of Solution’ of a substance. 
Ans:	It is the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance dissolves in 1.0 dm3 of a solvent under standard conditions of pressure and temperature (or at 298K and 100kPa).

PROBLEM OF THE DAY 12
Explain how the polygastric digestive system aids in digesting roughage.


Solution:

Animals with a polygastric digestive system have a multi-chambered stomach. 
The four compartments of the stomach are called the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum. 
These chambers contain many microbes that break down the cellulose and ferment the ingested food. 
The abomasum is the “true” stomach and is the equivalent of a monogastric stomach chamber where gastric juices are secreted. 
The four-compartment gastric chamber provides larger space and the microbial support necessary for ruminants to digest plant material.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY 13

Which internal structures of a plant can be an indication of whether a plant is C3 or C4? Explain.
Solution:
Leaves of C4 plants have Kranz anatomy, which makes them different from C3 plants. / The mesophylls are clustered around the bundle sheath cells in a ring-like fashion
C4 plants also have specialized cells called bundle sheath cells which surround the vascular bundles. 
Every cell of the bundle sheath has chloroplasts. 
The mesophyll cells of leaves of C4 plants do not differentiate into the spongy and palisade parenchyma possessing fewer intercellular spaces, while there is a normal occurrence of chloroplasts in the mesophyll cells. 
But in C3 plants, the bundle sheath does not exhibit chloroplast, and the mesophyll cells of the leaves are differentiated into the spongy and palisade parenchyma. 
Hence, by examining the internal structure, we can tell whether the plant is C3 or C4.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY 5

Define decomposition and describe the processes and products of decomposition.

Solution:
Decomposition can be defined as a process that involves the disintegration of complex organic matter from the body of dead animals and plants with the action of decomposers into inorganic raw materials such as water, carbon dioxide and other such nutrients. The different processes in decomposition are as follows:

Fragmentation – It is the first phase in the decomposition process, it includes the disintegration of detritus into fine particles through the action of detritivores such as earthworms.

Leaching – Here, the water-soluble nutrients penetrate the layers of soil and get sealed as unavailable salts.

Catabolism – Fungi and bacteria degrade detritus into fine particles through different enzymes.

Humification – This phase causes the formation of humus – a dark colored colloidal substance that serves as a reservoir of nutrients for plants.

Mineralization – Further degradation of humus through the activity of microbes takes place in this stage wherein inorganic nutrients are finally released into the soil.

In a form three class at a senior high school, the students were are asked to design an experiment to see whether vitamin A improves night vision.  They selected 100 general arts students and gave 50 of the students extra vitamin A for 6 weeks and then compared their night vision with that of the rest of the class. As a member of the science class explain the following
   (a) How you would select the group to be given the extra vitamin A
    (b) How would you standardize their intake of vitamins?
   (c) What tests would you conduct before giving the vitamin supplement?
   (d) How would you record and test the students’ night vision?
   (e) How would you analyze your results?                                                                                 

Answer
Initially, any student already taking vitamin A supplements would be excluded as well as students on a special diet. The group to receive the supplement would be selected at random, and the experimenter should not know which students were in which group. 
Students would be asked not to change their diet from their normal one during the course     of the experiment. Vitamin A tablets of a recommended dose would then be taken at intervals specified by a dietician or doctor. 
Students' night vision should be tested at the start of the experiment to establish a 'base line' for each student. 
A standard test card could be used, at a specified distance, in a dimly lit room not influenced by changes in the outside light intensity.  Left and right eyes would be tested separately. A method of scoring would have to be devised, e.g. the number of correct identifications, weighted for the size of type.  A standard time for students to become acclimatized to the dim light before starting the test would have to be decided. 
The mean score for each group would be calculated and the difference determined. It would then have to be judged whether this difference was significantly greater than the differences within either of the groups.

Use the Kinetic Theory of Gas to explain the following experimental observations: 
For a given gas at constant temperature and volume, the pressure increases when the molar quantity of the gas increases
Ans:	The Theory suggests that the pressure of a gas results from collision between the gas particles and the walls of the container. When the number of the particles increases, the number of collisions per unit area increases even at constant temperature.  
For a given amount of gas at a constant volume, the pressure of the gas increases with temperature. 
Ans:	A postulate of the Theory states that the average kinetic energy of a gas particle depends only on the temperature of the gas; hence the average kinetic energy increases as the gas gets warmer. For a gas, at constant temperature and pressure, the volume is proportional to the molar quantity. 
Ans:	As the number of gas particles increases, frequency of collisions with the walls of the container increases. As pressure in the container increases the volume of the container increases until the internal pressure and external pressure become equal.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY – 1.
Explain the following types of tropism in plants and indicate how they adapt plants to their habitats. Phototropism, Thigmotropism, Geotropism, Chemotropism, Thermotropism
 
Phototropism
Growth curvature in response to direction of light; enables plant shoots to grow and get light for maximum photosynthesis; allows for leaf mosaic. 

Thigmotropism
Growth curvature in response to contact/hard surface; makes plants with weak stems to get support on large plant/trees; this makes them to reach and get light for maximum photosynthesis. 

Geotropism. 
Growth curvature in response to gravity; enables plant roots to grow deep into the soil for maximum support/anchorage.

Chemotropism
Growth curvature in response to chemical concentration gradient; enables pollen tubes to grow down the style and into the ovary for fertilization to occur in seed plants (angiosperms and gymnosperms) / lateral roots in search of nutrients (positive) and roots growing away from harmful chemicals (negative)

Thermotropism
Growth curvature in response to temperature changes; enables plants to grow to where they can acquire optimum temperature for effective plant process (e.g. sunflower orientates towards the direction of the sun)

PROBLEM OF THE DAY – 2
Describe the genetic code and explain how it is “read”.  
The genetic code consists of the sequence of nitrogen bases in a polynucleotide chain of DNA or RNA (A, G, C, and T or U). 
The four bases make up the “letters” of the code. 
The letters are combined in groups of three to form “words” called codons. 
There are 64 possible codons, and each codon codes for one amino acid or for a start or stop signal. 
The codon AUG is the start codon that establishes the reading frame of the code. 
After the AUG start codon, the next three bases are read as the second codon. 
The following three bases after that are read as the third codon, and so on. 
The sequence of bases is read, codon by codon, until a stop codon is reached. UAG, UGA, and UAA are all stop codons.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY – 5
State Chargaff’s rules. Explain how the rules are related to the structure of the DNA molecule. 
There are two chargaff’s Rules.
Chargaff’s First Rule
Chargaff’s First Rule, often referred to as base pairing rule, states that in a double-stranded DNA molecule, the quantity of A (adenine) equals the quantity of T (thymine), and the quantity of G (guanine) equals the quantity of C (cytosine). 

This means that the total purine content (A + G) is equal to the total pyrimidine content (T + C). This base pairing is critical for the DNA's double-stranded structure and the stability of the DNA molecule.

Chargaff’s second rule
The second rule states that while the proportions of adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine may vary between different species, they remain consistent within a particular species. / the second rule stipulates that in any DNA molecule, the ratio of adenine (A) to thymine (T) and cytosine (C) to guanine (G) is approximately equal.
[For example, in humans, the base composition of DNA is approximately 30% adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine, and 20% cytosine. This rule emphasized the importance of understanding the unique characteristics of DNA for each species].
The uniformity in base pair ratios is central to the helical structure of DNA as the A-T and C-G base pairs fit together neatly within the double helix, maintaining a uniform width.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY MC 7 
You bought some naphthalene from a shop but you were informed that the naphthalene was contaminated with vinegar. Explain how you would obtain pure naphthalene. Heating the compound and collecting the cooled vapour will not get rid of the contents of vinegar.


Answer: 
The contaminated naphthalene is dissolved in a suitable organic solvent in a beaker 
The solution is transferred to a separating funnel 
Dilute NaOH/KOH solution (about 10 – 20 cm3) is added 
The mixture is shaken and the aqueous layer is separated from the organic layer 
The addition of NaOH/KOH solution and shaking are repeated a minimum of two more times 
The organic layer in the separating funnel is washed by adding de-ionised/ distilled water and thorough shaking 
The washing is repeated until the water separated is neutral to litmus 
The organic layer is transferred into a conical flask, and anhydrous MgSO4/drying agent added 
The organic layer is filtered into a round bottom flask and the solvent distilled off.
The residue is crystallised from a suitable solvent 
Pure naphthalene is stored in a labelled bottle

PROBLEM OF THE DAY MC 8 
Outline a method for separating about 300 cm3 liquid containing two organic, miscible liquids with boiling points 60 °C and 75 °C

Answer:
The liquid mixture is poured into a 500cm3 round bottom flask 
Some boiling chips are added 
A set-up for fractional distillation is placed on a water bath or in a heating mantle 
With the water running in the condenser, heating is started 
As the mixture boils, drops of liquid start collecting in the receiver 
When the temperature reaches 60 °C, the receiver is replaced with a new one
The fraction that boils at 60 °C is collected until there is no more 
Temperature may drop and rise again 
A new receiver is used to collect the fraction that boils at 75 °C 
Distillation is continued until there is only a small volume about (2cm3) left in the flask as distillation till the flask is dry is to be avoided.
The two liquids are stored in stoppered containers and appropriately labelled.
Note	i)	The volume of the round bottom flask should be stated since the liquid should not fill the flask to the brim.
	ii)	Distilling to the last drop should be avoided since such situations lead to explosions.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
List in sequence the mechanism through which a sound produces a nerve impulse in the inner ear.

SOLUTION

The ear is divided into three parts – the External ear, the Meddle ear and the Internal ear.
The external ear collects sound waves and drives them towards the tympanic membrane (ear drum).
The ear drum vibrates in response to the sound waves and these vibrations are transmitted to the oval window through the ear ossicles.  (Malleus, Incus and Stapes).
From the oval window, these vibrations are passed on the fluid of the cochlea, where they generate waves in the lymphs.
The waves in these lymphs generate ripples in the basilar membrane 
Movements of the basilar membrane make the “sensory hair” of the receptor cells in the organ of corti move in the overlying tectorial membrane and get distorted.
As a result of this stimulation, nerve impulses are generated in the associated afferent neurons.
These impulses are transmitted to the auditory cortex of the cerebrum, via. auditory nerves.
The auditory cerebral cortex analyzes these impulses and interprets them as sound.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

You are provided with about 2g of impure organic compound. The compound is contaminated with a little sand. You are also informed that ethanol is the most suitable solvent.
Describe, step by step, how you would perform recrystallization of the impure solid to obtain pure, dry crystals of the compound.

SOLUTION
Some volume of ethanol is poured into a conical flask and heated.
The impure solid is transferred into a beaker.
With the help of a glass rod a small volume ( <10 cm3) of ethanol  is added to the solid and the mixture stirred  (ie. solvent to solid).
More hot solvent is added in a small volumes and stirred until all the organic solid dissolves leaving particles of sand .
The hot solution is filtered through a fluted filter paper into a conical flask.
The flask is corked and put in the fridge or an ice-water bath.
After a while (several hours) the crystals and the supernatant are filtered using a fluted filter paper in a funnel or a filter flask and a Buchner funnel in suction filtration.
Some cold ethanol is used to wash the crystals, still on the filter paper in the funnel.
The filter paper with the crystal is transferred to a watch glass and this is kept on the bench or in an oven set at about 80oC. 
When crystals are dry, they are transferred with the use of a spatula into a sample bottle.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A girl frying an egg on an electric hot plate accidentally touches the hot plate, and quickly withdraws the hand from the plate. Explain this observation. 

SOLUTION

When the girl touches the hot plate, the sensory receptor in the skin receives the stimulus.
An impulse is then transmitted from the receptor to the spinal cord, via the dorsal root/sensory root.
The intermediate neurone in the spinal cord passes on the impulse to the motor neurone.
The motor neurone then sends the impulses to an effector organ (Muscle) via the ventral root.
The muscle upon receiving the impulse contracts causing the hand to be withdrawn from the hot plate.

A chemist needs 10 litres of a 40% hydrochloric acid solution. He has large quantities of 25% and 50% hydrochloric acid solutions. How many of the 25% acid solution and of the 50% acid solution should he mix to get the 10 litres of 40 % acid solution?



SOLUTION

x liters of the 25%  acid solution, and y liters of the 50% acid solution    

             x + y = 10     (volume of required 40 % acid solution)                                   (2 MARKS)

      0.25x + 0.50y = (0.4) 10     (volume of pure acid in the 10 litre acid solution)    (2 MARKS)

           25x + 50y = 400     (multiply by 100 to remove decimals)

               x + 2y  = 16              (divide by 25 to simplify above equation)                  (2 MARKS)

               x + y    = 10              (first equation)

                         y = 6           (subtract the above equations)                                        (2 MARKS)

                  x + 6 = 10, hence x = 4                                                                             (2 MARKS)

The chemist must mix 4 liters of the 25 % acid solution with 6 liters of the 50 % acid solution to obtain 10 liters of the 40 % acid solution.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

Ptyalinis a form of amylase found in saliva of humans and some animals. Another name of ptyalin is salivary amylase. It is a weak enzyme but the most important amylolytic enzyme secreted in the mouth (buccal cavity) by the salivary glands. Using the materials below, describe a simple experiment to show the action of the enzyme ptyalin.
2 test tubes, 10mls of 0.5% starch solution, 2mls of saliva, a clean glass rod, white tile, water bath, 5ml pipette, distilled water, stop watch, thermometer, iodine solution, Fehling’s solution. 

SOLUTION

Pipette 5mls of the 0.5% starch solution into each of the two test tubes.
Stand the two test tubes in the water bath maintained at 40oC.
To one test tube add some of the saliva, and to the other a similar volume of distilled water.
Using a glass rod, take a drop of the saliva/starch mixture after one minute on a white tile and add a drop of iodine solution.
Repeat step ‘4’ for the distilled water starch mixture.
Continue taking drops from each test tube until there is difference in the reaction of the two mixtures to the iodine solution.
When this happens, add few drops of the Fehling’s solution to the remains of each test tube.
The sample from the saliva/starch mixture will turn brick red while the distilled water starch mixture will pick the color (deep blue) of the Fehling’s solution. 
This shows that ptyalin in the saliva has broken starch down into maltose.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

A driver sets out on a journey to a town 60 km away and returns to base. For the first part of the journey, he drove at 90 km/hr to the town and for the return journey, he drove at    60 km/hr.  Find the average speed for the whole journey.



SOLUTION

Let time taken for the first half of the trip be T1

           T1 = 60/90 = 2/3 hr                                                                  (2 MARKS)

Let time taken for the return journey be T2

            T2 = 60/60 = 1 hr                                                                    (2 MARKS)

Total time for the whole journey T = T1 + T2 = 2/3 + 1 = 5/3 hr         (1 MARK)

Total distance covered D = 60 + 60 = 120 km                                      (1 MARK)

Average speed = total distance / total time                                         (2 MARKS)

                           = 120/(5/3) =  24 x 3= 72 km/hr                               (2 MARKS)

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
Without the use of internal metabolic mechanisms, explain how an ectoderm such as a lizard that lives on a hot desert environment is able to use behavioural mechanisms to regulate its body temperature on a daily basis.

SOLUTION:

The body temperature of the lizard in its real environment can be very different from its ambient temperature.
At night, when temperature drops to near freezing point, the lizard spends the night in a burrow where the soil temperature is constant.
In the morning when the air temperature is still cool, the lizard emerges from the burrow and achieves rapid rise in temperature by lying on a rock with maximum exposure to the sun.
The dark skin absorbs solar radiation causing the body temperature to rise far above the surrounding cool temperature.
In the afternoon, when the surrounding temperature is too high above that of the lizard’s body, it stays mostly in the shade, frequently in bushes, where there is a cooling breeze.
As the afternoon progresses, the air starts cooling and the lizard again spends much of its time in the sun on hot rocks to raise its body temperature.
The lizard returns to its burrow just before sunset, and goes through the same cycle the following day.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A girl spins round several times before stopping. When she stopped she continued to feel the sensation of spinning which made her feel dizzy a few minutes after stopping. Explain why spinning made her feel dizzy.

SOLUTION:

In addition to hearing, the ears do another important job. The inner parts of the ears (Semi-circular canals) give a sense of balance.
The inner parts are open spaces filled with fluid (gelatinous copula). The inside walls of the spaces are covered with tiny hairs. 
Each hair is connected to a nerve cell that carries signals to the brain. 
When the head moves, the fluid babbles/sloshes around and bends the hairs. 
As each hair bends, it makes its nerve cell send a signal, telling the brain about that movement.
When the girl spins around, the fluid starts spinning, too. That gives her the sensation of spinning.
 When she stops, the fluid keeps moving (and bending tiny hairs and signaling the brain). 
That makes her feel that she is spinning backward. We call that "feeling dizzy."

Problem of the day 7.										Round 3

State Newton’s First Law of motion. 
It is commonly observed that an everyday object at rest remains at rest whereas an everyday object propelled into motion usually comes to rest. Briefly explain each of these observations.
An object at rest on a horizontal surface is pushed by a horizontal force. It is observed that a greater effort is required to initiate motion of the object than to maintain its motion and the object stops moving when the effort is removed. 
Identify all forces acting on the object.
Briefly explain each of the observations indicated.

Problem of the day 7: Solution									Round 3

“Everybody remains in its state of rest or of motion with constant velocity unless compelled to do otherwise by external forces.”
An object at rest remains at rest if no net force acts on it. An everyday object propelled into motion is beset by dissipative forces (friction, drag, etc.) whose effect is to decrease the kinetic energy of the object to zero, thereby bring it to rest. All of this is in consonance with the First Law. Indeed, if dissipative forces could be eliminated entirely, an object propelled into motion will continue indefinitely in straight-line motion with constant velocity. 

The forces acting on the object are its weight, the normal force on it, friction, and the push.
The limiting static friction force is greater than the kinetic friction force so a greater effort is needed to overcome static friction and initiate motion that to overcome kinetic friction and maintain motion. If the effort is removed kinetic friction opposes the motion of the object until it comes to rest.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A dominant allele B confers black colour fur on certain breeds of dogs. If a dog is homozygous recessive (bb), it has white fur. Ernest would like to know whether his pet dog which has black colour is homozygous dominant (BB) or heterozygous (Bb). How might he determine the pet’s genotype?

SOLUTION:
Ernest could use a test cross to find if his pet’s genotype is either BB or Bb. He should allow his black dog to mate with a white dog (ie genotype bb). If any F1 offspring is white then the pet’s genotype is Bb. If the two parents are allowed to mate repeatedly, and all the offspring’s of the mating are black then there is a high possibility that his pet is BB. The greater the number of offspring, the more confident Ernest can be of his conclusion.

A closed rectangular box is made of thin cardboard 3x centimeters long and x centimeters wide. The volume of the box is 288 cubic centimetres.

Express the height h (centimeters) in terms of x
Express the total surface area, A square centimetres, of the box in terms of x. 
Find the value of x for which the A is least (minimum)

SOLUTION:

Let height of box be h centimetres
Volume of box V = 3x(x)h = 288, hence
h = 288/(3x2) = 96/x2							(2 Marks)

Surface area of box A = 2(3x)x+2(xh)+2(3xh)
=6x2+ 2x(96/x2) + 6x(96/x2)
=6x2+ 8x(96/x2) = 6x2+ 8(96)/x				        (4 Marks)

A= 6x2+ 8(96)/x
dA/dx= 12x – 8(96)/x2= 0	(minimum)			        (2 Marks)
12x3 = 8(96), hence x3 = 8(8) = 64
x=4								        (2 Marks)

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

You needed some naphthalene, a solid, for an experiment but were informed that the only sample available at the chemical store was contaminated with aniline.  You agreed to go for it and purify it.  Explain in detail how you would get rid of the aniline.


SOLUTION
Dissolve the impure naphthalene in a suitable organic solvent.
Add mineral acid, eg dil. HCl, about 10 -20% the volume of the organic solution in a separating funnel and shake the mixture.
Separate the organic layer from the aqueous layer 
Repeat the extraction of the aniline with mineral acid about two more times.
Wash the organic layer with small volume of deionized water.
Repeat the washing two or three times.
Dry the organic layer with anhydrous Na2SO4 or MgSO4
Filter off the solid.
Distill off the organic solvent till a residue of naphthalene is obtained.
Recrystallise  the crude naphthalene using a suitable solvent
Dry the crystals in a desiccator or spread over filter paper in the air.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
Most cells in living organisms are small in size. Explain what would happen if a round cell grows four (4) times wider than it normally would.

SOLUTION:

A physical relationship called surface-to-volume ration constraints increases in cell size.
By this relationship, an objects volume increases with the cube of the diameter, but surface area increases with the square.
The volume of this cell would increase 64 (43) times but the surface area only increases 16 (42) times. 
As a result, each unit of the cell’s plasma membrane must serve four times as much cytoplasm as it did previously. 
At certain point, the inward flow of nutrients and outward flow of waste will slow down leading to the death of the cell.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
You are provided with an organic solid for which the best solvent for its crystallization is ethanol. Outline a step by step procedure for obtaining dry crystals of the solid.

SOLUTION:

The solid is transferred into a beaker.
A small amount of the solvent is added to the solid (not solid to solvent).
The mixture is stirred while heating it on a water bath, some solid remains undissolved.
More solvent is added while stirring and heating continue.
The process is repeated until the solid dissolves in the minimum volume of hot solvent.
The hot solution is filtered through fluted filter paper to remove any impurities insoluble in ethanol into a conical flask
The hot solution is covered, and set aside to cool.
Crystals formed are filtered (by suction filtration).
The filtered crystals are washed twice with very cold ethanol.
The crystals are spread on a watch glass in the open air to allow the solvent to evaporate.
The crystals are transferred into a labeled bottle with a stopper.

You are provided with about 250 cm3 of a mixture of two organic solvents, one with a boiling point of 65oC and the other with a boiling point of 80oC.  Outline a method by which the two solvents can neatly be separated.
	
SOLUTION:
The liquid mixture is transferred into a 500 cm3 round bottom flask with a funnel.
A few boiling chips are added.
The flask is clamped over a water bath or in a heating mantle.
A fractionating column is connected to the flask, followed by a still head with a thermometer.
A water/Liebig condenser with a receiver adapter is attached.
With the water running in the condenser and a receiver in place, the heating of the water bath is started.
As the mixture boils drops of the first solvent collect in the receiver.
The temperature is watched and the moment it rises to 65oC the receiver is changed and the collection of the first solvent begins.
When all the first solvent distills off, the temperature drops.
The receiver is changed, the bath temperature increased and kept at a steady temperature until all the second solvent distills off.
The distillation is stopped when about 5 cm3 is left in the flask.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A girl spins round several times before stopping. When she stopped she continued to feel the sensation of spinning which made her feel dizzy a few minutes after stopping. Explain why spinning made her feel dizzy.

SOLUTION:

In addition to hearing, the ears do another important job. The inner parts of the ears (Semi-circular canals) give a sense of balance.
The inner parts are open spaces filled with fluid (gelatinous copula). The inside walls of the spaces are covered with tiny hairs. 
Each hair is connected to a nerve cell that carries signals to the brain. 
When the head moves, the fluid babbles/sloshes around and bends the hairs. 
As each hair bends, it makes its nerve cell send a signal, telling the brain about that movement.
When the girl spins around, the fluid starts spinning, too. That gives her the sensation of spinning.
 When she stops, the fluid keeps moving (and bending tiny hairs and signaling the brain). 
That makes her feel that she is spinning backward. We call that "feeling dizzy."

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
List in sequence the mechanism through which a sound produces a nerve impulse in the inner ear.

SOLUTION

The ear is divided into three parts – the External ear, the Meddle ear and the Internal ear.
The external ear collects sound waves and drives them towards the tympanic membrane (ear drum).
The ear drum vibrates in response to the sound waves and these vibrations are transmitted to the oval window through the ear ossicles.  (Malleus, Incus and Stapes).
From the oval window, these vibrations are passed on the fluid of the cochlea, where they generate waves in the lymphs.
The waves in these lymphs generate ripples in the basilar membrane 
Movements of the basilar membrane make the “sensory hair” of the receptor cells in the organ of corti move in the overlying tectorial membrane and get distorted.
As a result of this stimulation, nerve impulses are generated in the associated afferent neurons.
These impulses are transmitted to the auditory cortex of the cerebrum, via. auditory nerves.
The auditory cerebral cortex analyzes these impulses and interprets them as sound.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

You are provided with about 2g of impure organic compound. The compound is contaminated with a little sand. You are also informed that ethanol is the most suitable solvent.
Describe, step by step, how you would perform recrystallization of the impure solid to obtain pure, dry crystals of the compound.

SOLUTION
Some volume of ethanol is poured into a conical flask and heated.
The impure solid is transferred into a beaker.
With the help of a glass rod a small volume ( <10 cm3) of ethanol  is added to the solid and the mixture stirred  (ie. solvent to solid).
More hot solvent is added in a small volumes and stirred until all the organic solid dissolves leaving particles of sand .
The hot solution is filtered through a fluted filter paper into a conical flask.
The flask is corked and put in the fridge or an ice-water bath.
After a while (several hours) the crystals and the supernatant are filtered using a fluted filter paper in a funnel or a filter flask and a Buchner funnel in suction filtration.
Some cold ethanol is used to wash the crystals, still on the filter paper in the funnel.
The filter paper with the crystal is transferred to a watch glass and this is kept on the bench or in an oven set at about 80oC. 
When crystals are dry, they are transferred with the use of a spatula into a sample bottle.

Find two positive numbers whose sum is 100 and the sum of whose squares is a minimum.

SOLUTION
 Let the numbers be x and y

                     S = x2 + y2 is a minimum                                                      (1 MARK)

                     dS/dx = 2x + 2(x – 100) = 0 (since S is a minimum)        (2 MARKS)

                      d2S/dx2 = 4 > 0 so a minimum                                           (2 MARKS)
          Thus the numbers are x = 50 and y = 50                                        (2 MARK)

ALTERNATE SOLUTION (Using the method of completing the square)
                          x + y = 100                                                                         (1 MARK)
                S = x2 + y2 = x2 + (x – 100)2                                                        (2 MARKS)
                                  = x2 + x2 – 200x + 10000                                      
                                  = 2x2 – 200x + 10000                                       
                                  = 2(x2 – 100x) + 10,000                                           (2 MARKS)
                                  = 2[ (x – 50)2 – 2500] + 10,000

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A girl frying an egg on an electric hot plate accidentally touches the hot plate, and quickly withdraws the hand from the plate. Explain this observation. 

SOLUTION

When the girl touches the hot plate, the sensory receptor in the skin receives the stimulus.
An impulse is then transmitted from the receptor to the spinal cord, via the dorsal root/sensory root.
The intermediate neurone in the spinal cord passes on the impulse to the motor neurone.
The motor neurone then sends the impulses to an effector organ (Muscle) via the ventral root.
The muscle upon receiving the impulse contracts causing the hand to be withdrawn from the hot plate.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
A chemist needs 10 litres of a 40% hydrochloric acid solution. He has large quantities of 25% and 50% hydrochloric acid solutions. How many of the 25% acid solution and of the 50% acid solution should he mix to get the 10 litres of 40 % acid solution?



SOLUTION

x liters of the 25%  acid solution, and y liters of the 50% acid solution    

             x + y = 10     (volume of required 40 % acid solution)                                   (2 MARKS)

      0.25x + 0.50y = (0.4) 10     (volume of pure acid in the 10 litre acid solution)    (2 MARKS)

           25x + 50y = 400     (multiply by 100 to remove decimals)

               x + 2y  = 16              (divide by 25 to simplify above equation)                  (2 MARKS)

               x + y    = 10              (first equation)

                         y = 6           (subtract the above equations)                                        (2 MARKS)

                  x + 6 = 10, hence x = 4                                                                             (2 MARKS)

The chemist must mix 4 liters of the 25 % acid solution with 6 liters of the 50 % acid solution to obtain 10 liters of the 40 % acid solution.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

Ptyalinis a form of amylase found in saliva of humans and some animals. Another name of ptyalin is salivary amylase. It is a weak enzyme but the most important amylolytic enzyme secreted in the mouth (buccal cavity) by the salivary glands. Using the materials below, describe a simple experiment to show the action of the enzyme ptyalin.
2 test tubes, 10mls of 0.5% starch solution, 2mls of saliva, a clean glass rod, white tile, water bath, 5ml pipette, distilled water, stop watch, thermometer, iodine solution, Fehling’s solution. 

SOLUTION

Pipette 5mls of the 0.5% starch solution into each of the two test tubes.
Stand the two test tubes in the water bath maintained at 40oC.
To one test tube add some of the saliva, and to the other a similar volume of distilled water.
Using a glass rod, take a drop of the saliva/starch mixture after one minute on a white tile and add a drop of iodine solution.
Repeat step ‘4’ for the distilled water starch mixture.
Continue taking drops from each test tube until there is difference in the reaction of the two mixtures to the iodine solution.
When this happens, add few drops of the Fehling’s solution to the remains of each test tube.
The sample from the saliva/starch mixture will turn brick red while the distilled water starch mixture will pick the color (deep blue) of the Fehling’s solution. 
This shows that ptyalin in the saliva has broken starch down into maltose.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY

A driver sets out on a journey to a town 60 km away and returns to base. For the first part of the journey, he drove at 90 km/hr to the town and for the return journey, he drove at    60 km/hr.  Find the average speed for the whole journey.



SOLUTION

Let time taken for the first half of the trip be T1

           T1 = 60/90 = 2/3 hr                                                                  (2 MARKS)

Let time taken for the return journey be T2

            T2 = 60/60 = 1 hr                                                                    (2 MARKS)

Total time for the whole journey T = T1 + T2 = 2/3 + 1 = 5/3 hr         (1 MARK)

Total distance covered D = 60 + 60 = 120 km                                      (1 MARK)

Average speed = total distance / total time                                         (2 MARKS)

                           = 120/(5/3) =  24 x 3= 72 km/hr                               (2 MARKS)

PROBLEM OF THE DAY
Without the use of internal metabolic mechanisms, explain how an ectoderm such as a lizard that lives on a hot desert environment is able to use behavioural mechanisms to regulate its body temperature on a daily basis.

SOLUTION:

The body temperature of the lizard in its real environment can be very different from its ambient temperature.
At night, when temperature drops to near freezing point, the lizard spends the night in a burrow where the soil temperature is constant.
In the morning when the air temperature is still cool, the lizard emerges from the burrow and achieves rapid rise in temperature by lying on a rock with maximum exposure to the sun.
The dark skin absorbs solar radiation causing the body temperature to rise far above the surrounding cool temperature.
In the afternoon, when the surrounding temperature is too high above that of the lizard’s body, it stays mostly in the shade, frequently in bushes, where there is a cooling breeze.
As the afternoon progresses, the air starts cooling and the lizard again spends much of its time in the sun on hot rocks to raise its body temperature.
The lizard returns to its burrow just before sunset, and goes through the same cycle the following day.

Contest 17
How do plants regulate the turgor pressure in their cells?
Plants regulate the turgor pressure in their cells by directing water into specialized vacuoles. 
The vacuoles are hypertonic to the cytoplasm, so they draw water out of the cytoplasm. 
This allows the concentration of the cytoplasm to stay consistent, while the water is continually moved into the cell. 
As turgor pressure builds in the vacuole, it pushes out against the sides of the cell. 
Each cell is assembled so their cell walls are pushed together. In this way, each cell in a plant becomes a water filled brick. 
Plants can even turn their leaves and stems toward the sun by modifying the turgor pressure in their cells. 
If water is let out of the vacuole, the cell deflates.by changing the turgor pressure of a small group of cells.

Explain to a visual arts student in your school why we see objects more clearly in the dark when we look slightly to the side of the object. 
Answer
When looking directly at an object, light reflected from the object passes along the optical axis of the eye and strikes the retina at the fovea which contains cones only.
During daylight, this will produce a detailed image in the brain due to high light intensity activating the cones.
At night the light intensity will be too low to activate the cones
By looking slightly to one side of the object the reflected light from the object will not strike the fovea, but a point on the retina, to the side of it where there are rods.
At night, the rods will be activated by the low light intensity and an image will be produced in the brain

Ans:	As temperature increases, the kinetic energy of the particles in the gas

Ans:	When the volume of a given quantity of a gas is reduced, there is a 
		corresponding decrease in surface area so there is an increase in frequency 
		of collision of the particles with the surface although the speed of the 
		particles remain the same. More frequent collisions lead to increase in 
		pressure.

Ans:	Since particle sizes of gases are negligible compared to the volume, having 
		different particles in a given volume will not affect the movement and the 
		frequency with which each particle collides with the surface of the 
		container. Hence the total pressure will be the sum of the pressure each gas 
		would exert in the absence of others.

Ans:	Screening effect is the reduced attraction by the nucleus for the outermost electron caused by the core electrons.

Ans:	Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge that the outermost electrons feel through attraction by the nucleus.

c) Find the value of x for which A is a minimum.

d) Find the minimum value of A.

PROBLEM OF THE DAY 2018 FINALS   (POTD 13)

A salesperson for a furniture company can be paid in one of two ways for the furniture he/she sells.
PLAN A: a monthly salary of GHc900 plus a commission of 10% of sales
PLAN B: a monthly salary of GH1200 plus a commission of 15% of sales in excess of GHc8,000.
Assume that monthly sales always exceeds GHc8,000.  For what amount of monthly sales is

i) income from Plan A equal to that of Plan B? Find this monthly income.

ii) income from Plan B is better than that of Plan A?  


SOLUTION:
Let monthly sales be GHc x  where x > 8,000
Income from PlanA = 900 + 0.1x                                                 (1MARK)
Income from PlanB = 1200 + (0.15)(x - 8,000 )                         (1 MARK)

i) For equal incomes, we have
           900 + (0.1)x = 1200 + (0.15)(x - 8000 )                            (1 MARK)
                                 = 1200 – 1200 + (0.15)x
                                 = (0.15)x
                         900 = (0.05)x 
                            5x = 90000 and x = 18000                               (1 MARK)
The required monthly sales is GHc18,000                               (1 MARK)
The monthly income is 900 + (0.1)18000 = 900 + 1800 = GHc2700   (1 MARK)


ii) For Plan B to be better than plan A, we require

       1200 + (0.15)(x – 8000) > 900 + (0.1)x                                                    (2 MARKS)
                                    (0.15)x > 900 + 0.1)x
                                    (0.05)x > 900
                                            5x > 90000
                                              x > 18000                                                             (1 MARK)
Plan B is better than Plan A if monthly sales exceeds GHc18,000          (1 MARK)

Anassembly ofanextremely large number ofparticles which is

Thermodynamic system isclassified into thefollowing three systems

pressure, volume, temperature, internal energy andnumber ofmoles,
etc.These arecalled thermodynamic parameters orcoordinates or
variables.
The state variables may beextensive orintensive innature.
Extensive State Variables Extensive state variables depend onthe
sizeofthesystem, e.g.volume, total mass, internal energy etc.

depend onthesizeofthesystem, e.g.pressure, temperature and

1. During the electrolysis of dilute HCl using platinum electrodes, state the changes in the acidity 
of the electrolyte and explain why, the acidity of the solution changes.  
Answer:  The acidity increases (1 pt). The electrolysis of dilute HCl is equivalent to the 
electrolysis of water. As water is removed from the solution the concentration of HCl increases 
and hence acidity increases.  
2. Explain why there is a change in the colour of the solution during the electrolysis of CuSO 4 
solutions using platinum electrodes,  
Answer:  In the electrolysis of CuSO 4 solution using platinum electrodes, Cu2+ ions are 
discharged at the cathode whilst O 2 is discharge at the anode. The (blue) colour of the solution 
fades due to the reduction or removal of Cu2+ ions from the solution.  
3. State and explain the changes in the pH of the solution during the electrolysis of copper (II) 
tetraoxosulphate (VI) solution using inert electrodes.  
Answer:  The pH of the solution decreases (1 pt). This is because, as copper is discharged at the 
cathode, OH- is discharged as O 2 at the anode, leaving excess H+ in solution which increases 
acidity and decreases pH. Or water is discharged(removed) at the anode whilst Cu is deposited 
at the cathode. This increases the concentration of the solution, resulting in an increase in 
acidity and reducing/decreasing the pH of the solution.  
4. Explain why in the electrolysis of CuSO 4 solutions using copper electrodes the colour of the 
solution remains unchanged.  
Answer:  When copper electrodes are used, copper is deposited at the cathode. At the anode, the 
copper electrode decomposes into solution as Cu2+ ions, hence the concentration of Cu2+ 
remains constant and the colour remains the unchanged.

Explain why in the electrolysis of dilute HCl using inert electrodes, the acidity of the solution increases 
Ans:	Electrolysis of dilute HCl is equivalent to electrolysis of water. 
As water is removed from the solution the concentration of HCl increases and hence acidity increases
Explain why in the electrolysis of CuSO4 solutions using platinum electrodes the colour of the solution fades, but in the electrolysis using copper electrodes the colour remains the unchanged. 
Ans:	In the electrolysis of CuSO4 solution using inert electrodes, (Pt or C) Cu2+ ions are discharged at the cathode whilst O2 is formed by oxidation of water at the anode. The colour is due to the Cu2+ hence as it is removed from the solution, the colour fades. 
When copper electrodes are used, copper is deposited at the cathode as copper goes into solution at the anode, hence concentration of Cu2+ remains constant and the colour remains the same

Cost and Time Savings:
Video conferencing reduces travel expenses and time spent commuting, allowing for quick and efficient meetings. 
Enhanced Collaboration:
It facilitates real-time interaction and idea sharing, making it easier for teams to collaborate on projects. 
Improved Communication:
Visual cues and direct interaction can improve communication clarity and understanding. 
Accessibility:
Video conferencing allows individuals to participate in meetings regardless of location, promoting inclusivity and flexibility. 
Increased Productivity:
By eliminating travel and streamlining meetings, video conferencing can lead to increased productivity and efficiency. 
Better Engagement:
Video conferencing can be more engaging than audio conferencing, as participants can see each other and nonverbal cues. 
Record Keeping:
Many platforms offer recording features, allowing for easy review and documentation of meetings. 
Manage Live & Virtual Events:
Video conferencing allows companies to showcase their product line to a wide audience, strengthen relationships with existing customers and attract new ones 
Disadvantages:
Technical Issues:
Network problems, poor video or audio quality, and compatibility issues can disrupt meetings. 
Security Concerns:
Video conferencing platforms can be vulnerable to hacking and unauthorized access, posing security risks. 
Lack of Personal Interaction:
The absence of in-person interaction can make it harder to build relationships and foster trust. 
Non-Verbal Communication:
It can be difficult to pick up on subtle non-verbal cues that are important for effective communication. 
Time Zone Challenges:
Scheduling meetings across different time zones can be difficult and inconvenient. 
Initial Investment:
Setting up video conferencing infrastructure can require an initial investment in hardware and software. 
Fatigue:
Prolonged screen time can lead to fatigue and burnout. 
Privacy Concerns:
There are privacy concerns regarding the recording and sharing of video conference meetings.
